the bar chart illustrates the amount of waste disposed of through three different methods (landfills, burning and dumping at sea) in a European nation between 2005 and 2008

Overall, it is clear that while the amount of waste disposed of by landfill experienced a significant decrease, the opposite trend was true for burning. Additionally, dumping at sea remained relatively stable throughout the period.
As can be seen from the chart, landfill was the most popular method in 2005 at 1,800 million tonnes, but it dropped sharply to 600 million tonnes by 2008.
In contrast, burning grew steadily from 500 million tonnes to 900 million tonnes over the same period, overtaking landfill to become the leading waste disposal option in 2008.
Looking at the chart in more detail, dumping at sea remained the most stable method.
It started at 600 million tonnes in 2005 and hovered around this mark throughout the period.
By 2008, the figure for sea dumping stayed at 600 million tonnes, matching the amount recorded for landfill.

Overall, it is clear that the figures for most forms of transportation increased, except rail, which remained quite stable. Furthermore, roads were always the most popular, whereas pipelines were the least.
Starting with road transport, it was the highest in 1974, at approximately 70 million tonnes.
After that, it increased steadily, reaching nearly 100 million tonnes by 2002.
Water transport started at 40 million tonnes in the first year.
After increasing by 20 million tonnes 1982, it remained stable for the next 12 years.
Although it dropped slightly to 50 million tonnes in 1998, it quickly increased again and finished the period at over 60 million tonnes.
Meanwhile, pipeline transport experienced a gradual rise from nearly zero to over 20 million tonnes by 1982.
This figure then stayed the same for eight years and remained around 20 million tonnes until the end of the period, despite a small drop in 1994.
In contrast, rail transport fluctuated during the 28-year period, starting and ending at 40 million tonnes.
The bar charts illustrate the percentage of workers in Agriculture, Industry and Services and four countries in 1980 and 2010.

Overall, Germany, the USA, and Japan had similar trends, with Industry having the highest percentage of workers. In contrast, Agriculture was the largest sector in China. In addition, Industry grew in the first countries, while Services declined in all four nations.
In 1980, Industry was the biggest sector in Germany, the USA, and Japan, at 60%, about 52%, and 50% respectively.
By 2010, these figures increased significantly, reaching 80% in Germany, 78% in Japan, and 70% in the USA.
In contrast, the Services sector decreased in all three countries over the 30-year period, dropping to 40% in Germany, around 37% in the USA, and roughly 28% in Japan.
Agriculture had the lowest figures. Japan stayed below 12% in 1980 and fell below 8% by 2010.
In the USA and Germany, these figures are evenly smaller, from 9% down to about 5% in the USA and from 5% down to 2% in Germany.
In China, the trend was very different. In 1980, Agriculture had the highest proportion of workers at 70%, but this number fell sharply to 50% in 2010.
The figure for Services also dropped from nearly 50% to 20%.
On the other hand, the percentage of employees in Industry stayed unchanged at 40% in both years.
